children.html: Effects of Training Goals and Goal Orientation Traits on Multidimensional Training Outcomes and Performance Adaptability
Department of Human Resource Management, Rutgers University
Department of Management and Organizations, University of Iowa

We also examined the unique impact of the training outcomes on performance adaptability by predicting generalization to a more difficult and complex version of the task. The experiment involved 60 trainees learning a complex computer simulation over 2 days. The research model posited independent effects for training goals relative to goal orientation traits and independent contributions of training outcomes to the performance adaptability of trainees. The findings were consistent with the proposed model. In particular, self-efficacy and knowledge structure coherence made unique contributions to the prediction of performance adaptability after controlling for prior training performance and declarative knowledge. Many observers have noted the changing nature of work (Goldstein & Gilliam, 1991). Work is increasingly complex, entailing greater emphasis on cognitive skills. It is frequently mediated by computerized systems requiring organized domain-specific knowledge and confronting employees with heavy information-processing and decision-making demands. Furthermore, it is increasingly dynamic, placing a premium on the ability to generalize knowledge and skills, adapting them to new situations and problems (Kozlowski, 1998; Smith, Ford, & Kozlowski, 1997).

The increasing emphasis on knowledge and skill adaptability is broadening the traditional perspective of training theory and research. There are three key foci of this expanded perspective. First, it forces a broader conceptualization of training transfer. The traditional view considers transfer as a reproduction and maintenance of skills across environments, whereas the emerging perspective emphasizes the generalization and adaptation of knowledge and skills (Baldwin & Ford, 1988). That is, trained knowledge and skills need to be flexible, not rote, so they can be adapted to new, more difficult, and more complex situations (Schmidt & Bjork, 1992). Second, it expands the conceptualization of the criterion domain. Where traditional training design focuses on declarative knowledge and training performance as the principal learning outcomes, an expanded perspective includes indicators such as the structure of knowledge and self-efficacy to better capture a range of cognitive, behavioral, and affective development (Kraiger, Ford, & Salas, 1993). Third, it promotes a broader consideration of theoretically derived training interventions. Rather than the traditional focus on behaviorally based learning principles (e.g., overlearning, conditions of practice, reinforcement), scholars have noted the potential for advances in training design that may be derived from the application of theory that addresses the nature of trainee self-regulation, attention, and motivation (Ford, Smith, Weissbein, Gully, & Salas, 1998; Glaser, 1990; Smith et al., 1997; Tannenbaum & Yukl, 1992).
In regard to this last point, promising research has focused on interventions that promote active learning and affect the nature of self-regulation during

practice (Smith et al., 1997). Based on the work of Dweck (1986, 1989), Nicholls (1978, 1984), and others, training researchers have suggested that a goal orientation focused on mastering and learning new material, as opposed to demonstrating high levels of performance, has the potential to improve learning, self-efficacy, and performance (e.g., Gist & Stevens, 1998; Martocchio, 1994; Stevens & Gist, 1997; Winters & Latham, 1996).

Although this recent research on goal orientation-based training interventions is promising, it has generally been deficient in one or more of the key foci identified above. First, with few exceptions, it has rarely examined transfer of knowledge to new situations. Most of the research has focused on classroom settings where skill generalization is often not adequately assessed. Second, the research has often relied on a limited conceptualization and assessment of training outcomes, focusing most frequently on tests of declarative knowledge to index training effectiveness. Third, it has not simultaneously modeled the effects of individual goal orientation traits and other relevant individual differences, such as cognitive ability, that also influence learning and training effectiveness. This creates conceptual ambiguity as to the unique effects of instructional goals relative to the individual differences that trainees bring to training.

The present study contributes to the existing training research on goal orientation by addressing the deficiencies noted above. Principally, the current research distinguishes the independent effects of mastery and performance training goals and trait goal orientations on multidimensional training outcomes. These training outcomes include declarative knowledge, knowledge structure, training performance, and self-efficacy. Further, it models the effects of these multidimensional outcomes on performance adaptability for a generalization task that is substantially more difficult, complex, and dynamic. Kraiger et al. (1993) have called for research that elaborates the nomological network around cognitive, affective, and behavioral training outcomes. By examining a full spectrum of outcomes, and their theoretical influences, we begin elaborating linkages among individual differences, training interventions, learning, performance, and adaptability for complex dynamic tasks.

The research also provides for two more specific contributions to the training literature that focus on delineating training outcomes. First, the study examines self-efficacy and training performance as predictors of performance adaptability. Recent research has indicated that self-efficacy may be redundant with prior performance in the prediction of final training performance (Ackerman, Kanfer, & Goff, 1995; Mitchell, Hopper, Daniels, George-Falvy, & James, 1994). That is, self-efficacy does not explain unique variance in final training performance beyond that accounted for by prior performance, raising questions as to its usefulness as a training outcome. However, the literature suggests that self-efficacy may be an effective predictor of generalization (Gist & Mitchell, 1992). We examine self-efficacy for its unique contribution to the prediction of performance adaptability, after controlling for prior training performance. Second, this study examines the independent contributions of declarative knowledge and knowledge structure. Training research has typically examined measures of declarative knowledge as a primary learning outcome, neglecting

knowledge structure, which may be an indicator of deeper comprehension (Ford & Kraiger, 1995; Kraiger et al., 1993). Studies that examine knowledge structure, however, have not examined the relative contributions of knowledge structure and declarative knowledge for predicting performance adaptability. Both issues are examined in the context of an integrated examination of the influence of goal orientation on performance adaptability.

Goal orientation, in terms of learning and performance, has emerged in recent years as one of the more prominent influences in the educational and training research literatures. Of particular relevance, differences in goal orientation have been proposed to influence the nature and quality of skill acquisition and generalization (Dweck, 1986; Smith et al., 1997; Stevens & Gist, 1997). Although goal orientation was originally conceptualized in dispositional terms (e.g., Dweck, 1986; Nicholls, 1984), it is also subject to situational influences. This has yielded two different lines of research, each focusing on the learning, motivational, and performance implications of goal orientation. Work addressing goal orientation as a trait, and research examining goal orientationbased training interventions are described below.

Goal orientation traits. Several scholars have contributed to the development of the dispositional conceptualization of goal orientation (Eison, 1979; Dweck, 1986; Nicholls, 1984), represented by learning vs. performance-oriented traits. Although there are subtle differences among these perspectives, they can be traced to Atkinson's (1964) concept of achievement motivation and are united by this common foundation (Beaubien & Payne, 1999). The originators of goal orientation conceptualized it as a single bipolar trait (Dweck, 1986; Nicholls, 1984). More recent research has viewed learning and performance orientation as separate traits. In a rigorous series of four studies, Button, Mathieu, and Zajac (1996) provided convincing evidence supporting a twodimensional conceptualization.

Learning orientation is viewed as an adaptive response to novel or challenging achievement situations. Individuals with a learning orientation are thought to be attracted to such situations and approach them with an orientation toward self-improvement. They view their capabilities as malleable and believe that effort directed toward exploration and learning will yield self-improvement. They are resilient to challenge, persisting in the face of obstacles and failures. Errors and feedback are regarded as diagnostic of this improvement process and are used to aid learning. In contrast, performance orientation is viewed as a generally maladaptive response. Performance-oriented individuals seek easy situations that ensure positive evaluations of their capabilities, preferring to avoid novel or challenging achievement situations. Because they self-evaluate relative to others and view their capabilities as more stable, failure to achieve reflects negatively on the self. Thus, they seek to avoid errors and
negative feedback. Failure is associated with the withdrawal of attention and effort (see Dweck, 1986).

From a training perspective, goal orientation ought to be an important individual difference relevant to learning, motivation, and performance. Research generally supports this conclusion. For example, learning goal orientation has been associated with positive effects, and performance goal orientation with negative effects, on motivation to learn (Colquitt & Simmering, 1998), metacognitive activity (Ford et al., 1998), effort and the use of complex learning strategies (Fisher & Ford, 1998), feedback seeking (VandeWalle & Cummings, 1997), and self-efficacy (Chen, Gully, Whiteman, & Kilcullen, 2000; Phillips & Gully, 1997).

Goal orientation-based training interventions. Although goal orientation is often conceptualized as a trait, its theoretical foundation also recognizes that it can be activated by a variety of situational factors. Indeed, educational researchers view academic settings as complex situations containing a variety of salient cues that induce different goal orientations. Classroom settings that emphasize learning, effort, challenge, and errors as diagnostic feedback induce a learning or mastery orientation, whereas settings that emphasize the achievement of high grades and minimization of mistakes induce a performance orientation. For example, Ames and Archer (1988; Ames, 1992; Archer, 1994) assessed student perceptions of classroom characteristics, which were used to define mastery vs. performance orientations.

Rather than relying on student perceptions of classroom characteristics, training researchers have generally induced mastery (or learning) and performance orientations with deliberate manipulations. As one example, Martocchio (1994) created goal orientations by manipulating trainee conceptions of their ability, which is the underlying mechanism in Dweck's conceptualization of goal orientation. Trainees learning word processing software were induced to believe that their ability was malleable (mastery orientation) or fixed (performance orientation). Mastery orientations were created by informing trainees that practice makes perfect and that they should expect to make mistakes. Performance orientations were created by telling trainees that they should work smart using skills they already had.

More generally, however, training researchers have tended to follow the conceptual approach of educational psychologists (e.g., Ames and Archer, 1988) by manipulating a variety of cues consistent with either a mastery or performance orientation. For example, to induce a mastery orientation, Winters and Latham (1996) told trainees to identify a difficult and specific number of task strategies and to do their best on task outcomes. To induce a performance orientation, trainees were told to do their best identifying task strategies, but to attain a difficult and specific outcome goal. Thus, a mastery orientation was created by getting trainees to focus on learning strategies, whereas a performance orientation was created by getting them to focus on attaining task outcomes. In addition, goal levels were ramped to keep them at a constant level of difficulty. Similarly, Gist and colleagues (1990, 1991; Stevens & Gist,

1997; Gist & Stevens, 1998) have used complex manipulations designed to induce several underlying cues consistent with mastery and performance orientations. Their mastery intervention emphasized practice as a means for selfimprovement (Gist & Stevens, 1998; Stevens & Gist, 1997) and was also designed to influence the focus of self-regulation by affecting goals, cognitive monitoring, and strategies for improvement. Their performance intervention emphasized the achievement of outcomes and was consistent with goal-setting practices (e.g., Latham & Locke, 1991).

Results for goal orientation-based training interventions have tended to be consistent with the findings of trait-based research. Ames and Archer (1988) reported that mastery orientation was associated with reported increases in effort, the use of learning strategies, and challenge seeking. Performance orientation was generally not associated with outcomes (see also Ames, 1992; Archer, 1994). Martocchio (1994) reported that the malleable ability induction predicted higher computer efficacy and lower computer anxiety, although the fixed ability induction lowered computer efficacy for older trainees only. Age, computer anxiety, and computer efficacy predicted scores on a knowledge test following training, but these outcomes did not mediate the effects of the manipulations as predicted. Winters and Latham (1996) reported that for complex tasks, learning goals were better than outcome goals in terms of strategies identified and outcomes. Learning goals also yielded higher self-efficacy. Stevens and Gist (1997) indicated that mastery relative to performance-oriented trainees demonstrated more skill maintenance in transfer, planned to exert more effort, and evidenced less negative affect.

Although the research extending goal orientation to the training arena has generated findings consistent with its trait counterparts, it has generally been deficient in three key areas. First, it has rarely examined transfer, focusing most often on learning or training performance in a classroom setting. Transfer is one training outcome for which mastery and performance orientations ought to have differential effects. Some research has examined skill maintenance (Stevens & Gist, 1997) and generalization (Gist & Stevens, 1998) for more complex and dynamic tasks. However, it has treated generalization as a change in task content (i.e., shifting task content from salary negotiations to contract negotiations), but the application of the trained principles remained largely the same. Thus, we know relatively little about the ways in which goal orientation-based interventions influence performance adaptability under conditions of substantially increased task difficulty, complexity, and dynamics.

Second, goal orientation-based training research has often relied on a limited conceptualization and assessment of training outcomes. Indeed, some studies equate tests of declarative knowledge with performance (e.g., Martocchio, 1994), creating conceptual ambiguity regarding the distinction between knowledge and task performance and their differential effects. We need to consider a broader and more inclusive assessment of training outcomes (Kraiger et al., 1993) to evaluate the means by which goal orientation-based interventions achieve effects.
Third, research on goal orientation-based interventions has not modeled

the effects of individual goal orientation traits and other relevant individual differences such as cognitive or academic ability (e.g., Martocchio, 1994; Stevens & Gist, 1997; Gist & Stevens, 1998). Conversely, researchers examining goal orientation traits have not considered instructional goals (e.g., Phillips & Gully, 1997). This creates conceptual ambiguity as to the effects of instructional goals relative to the cognitive and dispositional individual differences that trainees bring to training. The potential for independent effects of goal orientation traits and goal orientation-based interventions remains to be established empirically.

The model guiding the present research is shown in Fig. 1. Goal-based models of learning, motivation, and performance incorporate self-regulation as a central process (e.g., Ames & Archer, 1988; Bandura, 1991; Kanfer, 1992; Karoly, 1993; Latham & Locke, 1991). At its most elemental level, self-regulation involves monitoring the differences between goals and current states. Negative discrepancies induce self-evaluation and, depending on affective and attributional reactions, reallocation of attention and effort to move closer toward goal accomplishment. Training goals are expected influence the nature of selfregulation during practice and to exhibit effects that are independent of goal orientation traits. Performance goals should orient the focus of self-regulation to improving performance scores during practice. Thus, performance goals should increase declarative knowledge, representing the basic information required for effective task performance, and task performance. In contrast, mastery goals should orient the focus of self-regulatory processes to the learning

the interrelationships of key task concepts and strategies. Thus, mastery goals should enhance knowledge structure, as a representation of deep comprehension, cognitive integration, and synthesis (Gist & Stevens, 1998). Mastery goals should also enhance self-efficacy, as an indicator of perceived competency and motivational resilience. The effects of training goals are expected to be distinct and independent of goal orientation traits. All the training outcomes are expected to predict adaptive performance. Of particular interest, however, are the unique contributions of knowledge structure coherence and self-efficacy. Although both outcomes have been examined in prior training research, the distinctiveness of (a) self-efficacy and final training performance and (b) knowledge structure and declarative knowledge are not well established. A more detailed rationale for linkages in the model follows.

The positive effects of cognitive ability on training are well established in the literature. Cognitive ability is the single best predictor of training effectiveness (Schmidt & Hunter, 1993), which is typically assessed via tests of declarative knowledge. Our purpose is not to question this expected effect. Rather, it is to establish that goal orientation traits have unique differential effects on training outcomes, independent of ability. Based on established findings, we expect ability to significantly predict the acquisition of declarative task knowledge.

As noted in the introduction, a growing body of research suggests that goal orientation traits affect learning styles and outcomes. Research results for trait performance orientation have tended to be inconsistent, sometimes exhibiting effects but more often failing to do so (Beaubien & Payne, 1999). Because trait performance orientation is presumed to focus self-regulation on the demonstration of competence, we hypothesize that it will exhibit a positive relationship with training performance. In contrast, a learning orientation is presumed to focus self-regulatory processes on self-improvement. Thus, we hypothesize that trait learning orientation will be positively associated with self-efficacy. When performance improves relative to standards, people develop a self-perception of task-specific competence. Moreover, self-efficacy has motivational implications (Mitchell et al., 1994). As individuals successfully iterate their accomplishments, expectations regarding their ability to further improve and handle challenges increase (Bandura, 1982). Individuals high in self-efficacy are more likely to persist when a task becomes difficult and challenging (Bandura, 1982, 1991; Gist & Mitchell, 1992).

Traditional training interventions orient trainees toward performance goals. The logic of this approach is that performance goals guide the trainee toward correct behavior in response to task stimuli, strengthening the bond between stimulus and response. Incorrect responses are discouraged because they weaken the desired bonds and interfere with learning. Although this traditional

behavioral approach has enjoyed wide application and considerable success, it may not be the most appropriate way to facilitate learning for complex tasks with heavier cognitive demands (Gist & Stevens, 1998; Winters & Latham, 1996).

Research indicates that an orientation to performance goals during skill acquisition may limit the availability of cognitive resources (Kanfer & Ackerman, 1989) and may hinder the learning of complex task relationships. As trainees attempt to maximize performance, they focus on a narrow set of surface characteristics (Meece, 1994) relevant to basic declarative knowledge. Thus, the focus of self-regulation is limited to superficial aspects of the task domain, preventing attention to deeper concepts and principles and inhibiting comprehension and knowledge integration. Trainees may exhibit good declarative knowledge and performance at the end of training, but may have a more superficial, rote form of learning. In addition, consistent failure to reach difficult performance goals may limit the development of self-efficacy (Stock & Cervone, 1990). When asked to perform under more complex transfer situations, trainees may lack the comprehension and resilience needed to generalize their skills to meet novel demands (Schmidt & Bjork, 1992).

Some researchers have suggested that some of the negative effects of difficult performance goals may be ameliorated by ramping the goals to keep difficulty constant as the individual learns (Winters & Latham, 1996). However, sequencing goal difficulty should not affect the focus of self-regulation around performance goals. Hence, the negative effects may be reduced but should be of the same quality (e.g., Winters & Latham, 1996). In summary, performance training goals are hypothesized to have independent effects on declarative knowledge and training performance at the end of training, but are not expected to evidence effects on other training outcomes (i.e., knowledge structure, self-efficacy, and adaptability).

In contrast, an orientation toward mastery goals may be more effective for the acquisition of complex skills (e.g., Ames & Archer, 1988; Gist & Stevens, 1998; Schunk, 1990; Stevens & Gist, 1997; Winters & Latham, 1996). Mastery goals focus attention on knowledge and skills needed for proficiency. They prompt a self-regulatory process focused on learning deeper task concepts and task relations (e.g., Brown & Pressley, 1994; Graham & Golan, 1991; Karoly, 1993; Nolen & Haladyna, 1990; Pintrich & Garcia, 1991). Mastery goals prime trainees to explore complex relations in the task, make errors, and learn from those errors. This promotes the development of a consistent organization of key task concepts (i.e., coherent knowledge structure) and task-specific selfefficacy. Moreover, learning theories indicate that complex skills build on the foundation of more basic knowledge (Fitts & Posner, 1967; Gagne, 1970), suggesting that mastery goals should be sequenced to orient attention to basic task features before shifting to more complex principles, such as task strategies and priorities.

In summary, mastery training goals are expected to yield positive effects independent of trait learning orientation. First, they should provide opportunities for trainees to engage in self-regulation centered on key task concepts,

strategies, and procedures as they endeavor to master successively more complex learning objectives. This is hypothesized to promote the development of a more coherent (i.e., consistent) knowledge structure (Smith et al., 1997). Second, mastery goals promote the view that skills are malleable (Martocchio, 1994) and errors are opportunities to enhance learning. As trainees monitor learning goal discrepancies, they are likely to perceive consistent improvements. This is hypothesized to yield increased self-efficacy (Bandura, 1991; Gist & Mitchell, 1992).

Baldwin and Ford (1988) distinguish two facets of training transfer, skill maintenance and generalization. Maintenance refers to the reproduction of trained skills in a new setting. Generalization refers to the adaptation of trained knowledge and skills to a more difficult and complex task situation (Ford et al., 1998). The two facets are related, in that maintenance is a necessary but not sufficient condition for generalization. Thus, declarative knowledge and performance achieved during training are both relevant to generalization by providing a foundation for skill maintenance. However, we believe that training outcomes of knowledge structure coherence and self-efficacy are particularly relevant to generalization. Knowledge structure coherence, an indication of the formation of a consistent knowledge organization, should help trainees comprehend the implications of changes in task rules and principles for relations with other task features. This should allow trainees to revise their strategies to adapt to the changed features. Self-efficacy should help trainees to be resilient in the face of increased task difficulty and challenge (Gist & Mitchell, 1992), providing them with a motivational boost and aiding adaptability.

The unique contributions of self-efficacy and knowledge structure coherence to the prediction of performance adaptability are key research issues. Training research has shown that self-efficacy generally loses its predictive potential when prior performance is controlled. It has been suggested that task-specific self-efficacy judgments are primarily influenced by prior performance during training such that self-efficacy and performance are redundant. According to this view, self-efficacy cannot be a significant predictor of performance once prior performance has been accounted (e.g., Mitchell et al., 1994). However, we believe that the motivational implications of self-efficacy are masked when one is trying to predict what is essentially skill maintenance. When trying to predict generalization, the unique effects of self-efficacy beyond prior performance are expected to be significant because they will enhance self-regulatory resilience when tasks become challenging.

Similarly, research has shown knowledge structure to be a significant predictor of subsequent performance (Acton, Johnson, & Goldsmith, 1994; Dorsey, Campbell, Foster, & Miles, 1999; Kraiger, Salas, & Cannon-Bowers, 1995; Stout, Salas, & Kraiger, 1997). However, two issues need to be addressed. First, with one exception (Stout et al., 1997), prior work has not examined the extent to which knowledge structure and declarative knowledge capture distinct forms

of learning. Second, prior work has tended to examine subsequent performance in terms of skill maintenance, not generalization. It is not known whether knowledge structure contributes to adaptive performance. Thus, if these learning outcomes provide the foundation for adapting knowledge and skills to more difficult and complex situations, they should account for unique variance in performance adaptability after controlling for prior effects in the model. The unique relevance of knowledge structure coherence and self-efficacy can be ascertained by controlling for declarative knowledge and training performance.

Trainees were students at a large midwestern university (N 5 68) recruited from undergraduate psychology courses. They received nominal course credit for participation in the 5-h experiment. Eight trainees had incomplete data due to hardware or software difficulties (n 5 6) or failure to follow the experimental procedure (n 5 2). Data for these cases were deleted from all analyses. The analysis sample consisted of 60 trainees.

Design. The research employed a mastery vs. performance training goal manipulation, with training sequenced through four trials. There were two trials on each of 2 consecutive days, with each set of two trials comprising a session. Training goals were sequenced to emphasize more advanced learning objectives (mastery) or increasingly higher scores (performance). The conclusion of training was followed by a generalization trial in which task difficulty increased, and task principles were modified to make the task more complex. This provided a means to assess the extent to which trainees could adapt their knowledge and skills to a more difficult and complex task condition.

Complex task. The research employed a version of a PC-based decisionmaking simulation (TANDEM; Weaver, Bowers, Salas, & Cannon-Bowers, 1995) used for research and training (Inzana, Driskell, Salas, & Johnston, 1996). The task enacted a dynamic information-processing environment by simulating a radar-tracking task. Participants were seated at a computeremulated radar console that displayed multiple contacts. The task was to select a contact traversing the screen, access cues, identify its characteristics, and determine its final disposition. This required the participant to collect up to 5 cues, each with 3 values, for each of three subdecisions (15 cues 3 3 values overall) and to then render an overall engagement decision (clear or shoot). Participants had to learn the cues, cue links to subdecisions, and the decision sequence to perform correct engagements. They received points for correct decisions and lost points for incorrect decisions. In addition to these information-processing demands, complex relations were embedded in the scenario that necessitated shifts in task priorities and strategies. Participants had to

defend two perimeters, one visible inner perimeter and one invisible outer perimeter, from contact intrusions that also cost points. Fast moving and "popup" contacts that appeared suddenly near perimeters affected task dynamics, priorities, and strategies. In summary, TANDEM provides a complex, selfcontained, and novel task environment appropriate for the examination of complex skill acquisition.

Task information. Trainees received a brief overview and demonstration of the simulation. They were informed that they would progress through four 15 min practice training trials and would then have an opportunity to show how much they had learned on a more difficult and complex version of the task. Each training trial was preceded by a 10-min study period in which the manipulations were presented, and trainees were instructed to read the simulation manual and other training materials.

A central concern during the design of the experiment was to ensure that observed differences could not be attributed to differences in access to training content. Several steps were taken to ensure that performance goal trainees had access to identical knowledge emphasized in the learning objectives. First, an operating manual for the task was examined by all participants prior to the interventions. It provided detailed explanation of the task, including any information relevant to learning objectives. Second, all trainees had the manual available for the study period prior to each practice trial. They were instructed to study the manual and any other materials they received. Third, the manual was available for consultation throughout practice. All subjects were instructed to consult the manual as necessary at any time during the practice trials. Thus, both training conditions were given access to exactly the same task information.

Feedback. Diagnostic decision feedback was available to all trainees during training trials. Trainees simply held down the button on their mouse as they rendered the Engage decision to see whether they were correct or incorrect on any of the four subdecision components and its effect on their score. In addition, the radar screen continually displayed their cumulative score for a trial.

Incentives. To induce effort, trainees were informed that prizes were to be awarded for (a) questions answered during the training phase and (b) performance on the final transfer trial at the end of the second session. Instructions were carefully worded to prevent conflict with the training manipulations. Instructions for answering questions were deliberately vague and made no direct reference to learning. The purpose was to make sure trainees were attentive when responding to measures of individual differences, manipulation checks, and learning outcomes.

Performance adaptability. The transfer task was designed to require generalization of the knowledge and skills acquired during training. Design was guided by Wood's (1986) typology of task complexity to ensure a substantial increment in difficulty and complexity elements. Following the training, trainees received instructions that described important task differences they would now encounter. All trainees received a performance goal that they were to

accomplish. In addition, diagnostic decision feedback was turned off during the transfer task, although the cumulative score indicator remained on the screen to allow trainees to monitor their progress.

To increase difficulty, the transfer scenario (1) contained a 30% increase in the number of contacts (60) and (2) trainees were told that points would be deducted if they did not engage a specified number of contacts (45), although no points were actually deducted. Given that well-practiced task experts had difficulty processing 30 contacts in the time allotted, this represented a substantial increase in difficulty. To increase task complexity, the scenario (1) contained more "pop-up" contacts, (2) changed the rules such that substantially more penalty points were assessed for inner (2100 points) and outer (250 points) defense perimeter intrusions, and (3) increased task dynamics by increasing the number of intrusive contacts. The changes in task complexity and difficulty ensured that trainees had to adapt previous knowledge and skills to meet the demands of the new situation. Furthermore, the transfer scenario required resilience in order to maintain motivation and concentration throughout the session.

The construction of the manipulations was consistent with prior research on goal orientation-based training interventions in that multiple cues were used to induce the desired orientations (e.g., Gist & Stevens, 1998; Stevens & Gist, 1997; Winters & Latham, 1996).

Performance goals. Participants were instructed that their purpose was to perform at their maximum during the study. They were oriented to achieve a difficult and specific level of performance during each trial. The importance of achieving their score goals and maximizing correct decisions was emphasized. They were told to minimize incorrect decisions, because each incorrect decision would take an extra correct decision to get them back to the same score. They were instructed to monitor their cumulative score as an indicator of their level of performance achievement relative to their goal.

Trainees were presented with a performance goal prior to each training trial that specified the score that they were to achieve during the trial. Goals were sequenced to increase across trials (e.g., Winters & Latham, 1996). During initial skill acquisition on complex tasks, the large discrepancy between initial performance and a difficult terminal goal can undermine performance (Kanfer & Ackerman, 1989) and self-efficacy (Gist & Mitchell, 1992). Thus, performance goals were sequenced at the 85th percentile for each trial based on pilot data—(1) 590, (2) 1140, (3) 1340, and (4) 1840 points—to reduce the discrepancy between goals and performance (e.g., Earley, Connolly, & Ekegren, 1989). This approach was taken to ameliorate some of the negative effects of performance goals on learning (Stock & Cervone, 1990). Although this potentially weakened the difference between the mastery and performance conditions, it provided a more rigorous evaluation of mastery goal effects.

Mastery goals. Participants were advised that their purpose was to learn, understand, and master the simulation. They were oriented to explore a sequence of learning objectives, to use errors as learning opportunities, and to use their scores as diagnostic feedback. They were told that they should focus on the learning goals, using them to guide their learning, practice, and skill development. They were advised to think about their score as feedback that could help them to learn about the game.

Trainees were presented with mastery goals prior to each training trial. Mastery goals were sequenced from basic task knowledge (Session 1; Trials 1 and 2) to more advanced strategies (Session 2; Trials 3 and 4). Session 1 emphasized the importance of learning cue values, their links to subdecisions, and the overall decision sequence. Learning how to deal efficiently with ambiguous cues was also emphasized. Session 2 shifted to more complex aspects of the task, such as assessing the broad situation and anticipating trouble and establishing priorities and making strategic trade-offs. The mastery goals focused trainee attention on learning, but all task information was contained in the training manual and was accessible by trainees in both training conditions. Thus, differences across conditions could not have been due to differential access to relevant task information.

Individual differences. Assessments were collected prior to the manipulations and experimental trials. Grade point average (GPA) indexed academic achievement and is regarded as a suitable indicator of the studying ability needed for learning (e.g., Thomas & Mathieu, 1994). Trait measures of learning and performance orientation allowed us to determine the contribution of the individual differences relative to the manipulated conditions. The orientations were assessed using a randomized set of 16 items (Button et al., 1996). Responses were made using a 5-point format ranging from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (5). The coefficient a was .85 for the learning and performance orientation measures.

Goal commitment. A seven-item measure of goal commitment was employed as a manipulation check on the mastery and performance training goals. It was assessed at the end of each of the four study periods (postmanipulation), prior to the start of the corresponding practice trials. Items were from the measure by Hollenbeck, Williams, and Klein (1989), with minor modifications to make it appropriate for the simulation. Responses were made using a 5-point format ranging from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (5). Coefficient a reliabilities across all trials exceeded .90.

Declarative knowledge. Assessments of declarative knowledge were obtained at the end of training. The measure was composed of 15 multiple-choice items used to assess factual knowledge relevant to operating the task (Nason, Gully, Brown, & Kozlowski, 1995). These test items posed questions about basic task knowledge, such as cue type–value–decision linkages, and basic operating
features of the task, such as hooking contacts, accessing cues, and changing range.

Knowledge structure coherence. Assessments of knowledge structure coherence were obtained at the end of training. Trainees indicated the relatedness of pairs of 16 task concepts (9 basic, 7 advanced) using a 0 (no similarity) to 9 (highly similar) scale. The Pathfinder algorithm (Schvaneveldt, 1990) was used to compute the coherence, an index of consistency, of trainee knowledge structures. For example, if concept A is related to concept B, and concept B is not related to concept C, concepts A and C should also have no relation. Thus, high coherence signifies the formation of a consistent knowledge structure of concepts and their interrelations. Low coherence indicates inconsistency among concept relations.

Self-efficacy. Self-efficacy was measured at the end of training. It was operationalized as a task-based self-perception, with item content specifically focused on the ability to cope and to develop methods to effectively deal with the information, decisions, and challenges of the simulation. This operationalization is consistent with conceptualizations of self-efficacy as a central component of the self-regulatory process that view the construct as a task-referenced selfevaluation of capability (Gist & Mitchell, 1992). It was assessed using an eightitem self-report measure developed for this research. Responses were made using a 5-point format ranging from "strongly disagree" (1) to "strongly agree" (5). The coefficient a for the measure was .95.

Performance. Performance was assessed using scores generated by the simulation at the end of training and during the generalization trial. Evaluation of the model necessitated composite performance criteria that combined both the basic and strategic elements of the task—engage contacts correctly and avoid defense perimeter intrusions. These same composite scores were used as goals and to provide cumulative score feedback to participants during the training and transfer trials. The training performance composite was 100 points for correct, 2100 for incorrect decisions, and 210 points for inner and outer perimeter intrusions. The performance generalization composite was 100 points for correct, 2100 for incorrect decisions, 2100 points for inner, and 250 points for outer perimeter intrusions.

Preliminary analyses indicated the effectiveness of the goal manipulations. Trainees were committed to their assigned goals (means of 4.0, 4.0, 3.9, and 3.9 for trials one through four, respectively) and there were no significant differences in goal commitment across the goal conditions. Goal commitment did not significantly interact with mastery or performance training goals in the prediction of performance. Thus, goal commitment and potential interactions were excluded from subsequent analyses.

The research model illustrated in Fig. 1 was evaluated. Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, and intercorrelations, are shown in Table 1. We included one-tailed tests because we had strong directional hypotheses and because a power analysis indicated that power equaled .67 for r 5 .30 with a two-tailed test (p # .05), whereas a one-tailed test yielded power of nearly .80 (Cohen, 1988, 1992). We evaluated the tenability of the proposed model in Fig. 1 by examining its overall fit as well as testing each of the individual links in the model. Thus, we considered the unique contributions of learning and performance orientations, training goals, and ability to the prediction of declarative knowledge, knowledge coherence, training performance, and self-efficacy. We also investigated the contributions of the training outcomes to the prediction of performance adaptability. These analyses allowed us to evaluate the plausibility of training outcomes as mechanisms through which individual differences and training variables influenced adaptability.

Ability, indexed by academic achievement, was expected to influence declarative knowledge as a traditional outcome of training effectiveness. Trait goal orientation and goal orientation-based training were expected to affect the focus of self-regulation, with impacts on declarative knowledge, performance, knowledge structure coherence, and self-efficacy. Trait performance orientation and performance training goals were expected to enhance training performance and declarative knowledge. Mastery goals, in combination with declarative knowledge, were expected to improve knowledge structure coherence. Mastery goals, trait learning orientation, and training performance were expected to enhance self-efficacy. Finally, each of the four training outcomes was expected to influence adaptive performance. Training outcomes important to adaptive performance included declarative knowledge, knowledge structure coherence, training performance, and self-efficacy.

As we conducted our analyses, there were three primary issues of interest. First, we were interested in assessing the effects of individual differences and training goals on training performance, declarative knowledge, knowledge coherence, and self-efficacy. In particular, we evaluated the unique contribution of learning and performance orientation traits in combination with mastery and performance training goals. Although previous studies have examined the effects of either training goals or individual differences alone, very little research has examined the effects of both in combination.

Second, we evaluated the unique contribution of self-efficacy to the prediction of adaptability after controlling for previous performance- and knowledge-based measures. This provided a particularly stringent test of self-efficacy's effects on adaptability because self-efficacy is known to be correlated with previous performance and knowledge. Thus, partialling knowledge and performance variables reduced the variation in adaptability that could be uniquely explained by self-efficacy.

Third, we investigated the prediction of adaptability using knowledge structure coherence after controlling for previous performance, declarative knowledge, and self-efficacy. Previous research has examined the effects of knowledge structure on performance, but these investigations have not determined

We performed an overall evaluation of our model using the path analytic procedures described in Pedhazur (1982) and Cohen and Cohen (1983). Path analysis was selected over structural equations modeling (SEM) because when sample sizes are small the standard errors in structural equation models are essentially unknown (Bentler, 1993; Chan, 1998; Raykov & Widaman, 1995), unless overidentifying restrictions are placed to make it essentially equivalent to conducting a path analysis.

Each endogenous variable was regressed on all variables with paths leading to it. The coefficients obtained from each regression provided path estimates. The t test for each regression coefficient indicated whether a particular path was significant. As shown in Fig. 2 and Table 2, with the exception of the paths from performance orientation to training performance, and training goals to declarative knowledge, all paths were significantly different from 0.

Next, we regressed training performance onto trait performance orientation and declarative knowledge. We predicted 29.3% of the variance in training performance, F(2,57) 5 11.81, p # .01. We then regressed declarative knowledge onto ability and training goals. We predicted 21.7% of the variance in declarative knowledge, F(2,57) 5 7.998, p # .01. Test of overall model fit. As seen in Table 2, nearly all of the path coefficients were significant, providing initial support for our theoretical model. It should be noted, however, that it is possible for a model to be misspecified even if each of the path coefficients is significant. The omnibus test of model fit addresses this issue. The omnibus test of the overall fit of the model relies on the difference in fit between the just-identified model (which will perfectly reproduce the correlations) and the overidentified model (which will exhibit lack of fit to the degree that the model is wrong). This test is based on the generalized squared multiple correlation (R2 full) which is conceptually the average variance explained across the endogenous variables in a just-identified model. The following equation represents the R2 full: R2 full 5 1 2 (1 2 R2 1)(1 2 R2 2)(1 2 R2 3)... (1 2 R2 k).

In order to compute R2 full, we added all nonhypothesized links to the model to obtain a just-identified model in which the predicted variance in the endogenous variables is maximized. We obtained 0.945 for R2 full using the just-identified model. Next we computed the average variance explained using our hypothesized (reduced) model. Our reduced model retained only our hypothesized links, and it yielded a generalized R2 reduced value of .935. The test of model fit is based upon the Q statistic, which is defined as (1 2 R2 full)/(1 2 R2 reduced ). The Q ratio is a ratio of the residual of the generalized R2 fullto the residual of the generalized R2 reduced and it varies from 0 to 1. The closer Q is to 1, the better the fit of the model to the data (Pedhazur, 1982, p. 620). We obtained a Q of 0.856, indicating that our model fit the data well. The x2 value for goodness of fit was computed using the formula x2 5 2(N 2 df)logeQ. We obtained a nonsignificant x2 (6.701, df 5 17, p . .90). Thus, the results of the omnibus test of model fit indicated that our hypothesized model fit the data well.
To ensure that the selection of path analysis as our analytic technique did

not influence our conclusions, we also estimated the fit of the path model with LISREL 8.3 using generalized least squares. Generalized least squares (GLS) were employed because Hu and Bentler (1998) found that GLS estimates for the RMSEA, GFI, and AGFI fit indices were more accurate than maximum likelihood estimates (ML). Additionally, Sugawara and MacCallum (1993) found that ML and OLS estimates indicated better fit of a given model than GLS estimates, possibly leading to overacceptance of hypothesized models. For completeness, we also ran the model using maximum likelihood estimates and obtained very similar results to the path analysis. All paths that were significant using GLS remained significant using ML, and the x2 for goodness of fit was nonsignificant and of similar magnitude. The overall fit of the model was consistent with the path analysis results, and the fit of our model to the data was strong (x2 5 11.21, df 5 17, RMSEA 5 0.01, GFI 5 .97, AGFI 5 .92). We also performed path analysis and LISREL analyses using a natural log transformation of performance because the cognitive literature shows that learning can follow a power function.1 The findings were virtually identical. Finally, we tested a LISREL model in which we added error to each of the observed variables using reliability estimates to ensure that measurement error did not bias our findings. The results were similar to those of all other analyses.

Academic achievement, as an indicator of ability, made a significant contribution to declarative knowledge. As in much prior research, performance orientation was not significantly related to training performance, thereby providing no support for its expected effects. Learning orientation was significantly related to self-efficacy, as expected. Overall, individual differences generally demonstrated their expected contributions

Mastery goals evidenced a significant positive effect on knowledge structure coherence in combination with declarative knowledge. This is consistent with the theoretical relations illustrated in the model, suggesting that basic declarative knowledge is the foundation for more advanced forms of knowledge organization. Mastery goals, by prompting self-regulation toward learning key task concepts, contributed to the development of knowledge structure coherence. Mastery goals also had a significant positive effect on self-efficacy in combination with learning orientation and training performance. Thus, there is general support for the proposed effects of trait learning orientation and mastery training goals. Performance goals did not evidence expected effects on declarative knowledge or training performance.

Performance adaptation. The model accounted for 73.2% of the variance in performance adaptation, with each of the learning outcomes making significant contributions. As expected, training performance made the largest contribution to prediction, followed by declarative knowledge. After controlling for all other

The current study expands our understanding of how individual differences, training interventions, and training outcomes influence performance adaptability in several important ways. First, we include a broader conceptualization of training transfer than typically found in research. Our perspective emphasizes the generalization and adaptation of knowledge and skills to new, more difficult, or more complex situations. Second, as a result of the first point, our focus includes multidimensional training outcomes. This expanded perspective focuses on the unique impacts of declarative knowledge, organization and structure of knowledge, self-efficacy, and training performance on adaptability. Finally, we elaborate how individual differences and training design together may influence trainee self-regulation, learning, and motivation.

Theoretical progress in training design necessitates a more integrated conceptualization of individual differences, training, and learning outcomes than is typical in training research (Kraiger et al., 1993). In the present case of skill acquisition for complex tasks, a model was developed to specify this integrated conceptualization. In particular, learning outcomes that extend beyond basic declarative knowledge and training performance were specified to better capture the effects of self-regulation toward learning objectives, transfer, and adaptability. The main purpose was to demonstrate that training designed to influence the focus of self-regulation would enhance trainee generalization in a more difficult and complex task situation. In this way, we hoped to enhance understanding of the learning process and the means by which training can leverage improvements in skill acquisition for complex tasks.

Our conceptual model identified four primary learning indicators, including training performance, declarative knowledge, knowledge structure, and selfefficacy, that we believed would be affected by training goals and goal orientation traits. Mastery goals were conceptualized as affecting the focus of selfregulatory processes that would promote a deeper comprehension of task complexities and interrelations. In combination with trait learning orientation, mastery goals were expected to influence the development of knowledge structure coherence and self-efficacy. We also hypothesized that multidimensional learning outcomes would facilitate adaptation by providing unique contributions to the prediction of performance generalization to a more difficult and complex task situation.
Results for the integrated analyses are consistent with the theoretical model.

Individual differences in ability and learning traits made significant differential contributions to the different learning outcomes, although the performance trait had no demonstrable impact. Training made contributions independent of the individual differences. Ability had a primary effect on declarative knowledge. Mastery training goals had primary effects on knowledge structure coherence and self-efficacy. They combined with declarative knowledge to affect knowledge structure coherence. This is consistent with theory that indicates declarative knowledge is an essential foundation for the development of a deeper comprehension of task relations. Mastery goals, by focusing self-regulation on key learning objectives, provided an additional unique contribution to the development of knowledge coherence. In addition, mastery goals, in combination with training performance and trait learning orientation, influenced self-efficacy. By orienting trainees to self-regulate toward specific learning objectives, mastery goals facilitated the development of a self-perceived capability to deal with task challenges.

Another important contribution is that we demonstrated that different training outcomes each provide unique contributions to the enhancement of performance adaptability. Previous research has typically focused on only one or two training outcomes at a time. However, if one does not measure and assess multiple outcomes then it becomes difficult to disentangle their relative importance. It is not difficult to show that any one training outcome can, by itself, predict later maintenance and generalization. For example, one can show that declarative knowledge relates to later performance. However, we can be fairly sure that declarative knowledge is related to previous skill and performance, so it is possible that declarative knowledge relates to subsequent performance merely because it is a surrogate for previous performance. The question thus becomes, "does declarative knowledge add any unique prediction to generalization after controlling for previous levels of skill or performance?" Our findings make a strong statement that multiple outcomes are important for generalization and adaptability.

Performance adaptability was independently predicted by all four learning outcomes: training performance, declarative knowledge, knowledge structure, and self-efficacy. In addition to the presented analysis, we performed supplementary analyses in which we assessed the unique impact of these four outcomes after controlling for all causally prior variables in the conceptual model. It is noteworthy that these significant effects remained after controlling all prior effects in the model, including the individual difference measures and training goals. In addition, the contributions for the learning outcomes influenced by mastery goals—knowledge structure and self-efficacy—were assessed after controlling for the well-established effects of training performance and declarative knowledge.

On a related point, previous research has debated the unique importance of self-efficacy as a determinant of subsequent performance. Some researchers have found that self-efficacy predicts no unique variance in subsequent performance after controlling for previous performance (e.g., Ackerman et al., 1995; Mitchell et al. 1994). For example, Mitchell et al. (1994) state,

''Examination of these sets of correlations demonstrates that, without exception, the best predictor of current performance was past performance...the inclusion of past performance in a regression equation resulted in a large significant regression weight for past performance and small, nonsignificant weights for self-efficacy and expected score.''

As a result of such findings, some might argue that self-efficacy is nothing more than a self-reported surrogate for actual levels of ability. Similarly, because selfefficacy is likely to be related to one's actual levels of knowledge, one might argue that self-efficacy is a surrogate for what one knows about the task. From our perspective, however, self-efficacy is a self-assessment of current and future capability that can influence motivational and regulatory processes during and after training. In particular, these processes should manifest themselves when trainees face complex or difficult situations. Indeed, this is exactly what we found. When faced with a more challenging task, self-efficacy made significant contributions to the prediction of performance adaptability even after controlling for previous performance, declarative knowledge, and knowledge structure coherence. How can we reconcile these findings with previous findings? We believe the difference is due to varying levels of task-induced motivation and self-regulation. When task demands and characteristics are static, it stands to reason that previous performance and self-efficacy become increasingly redundant predictors of performance and that prior performance will be the superior predictor. However, when task demands evolve, then although previous performance will be related to subsequent performance, motivational and self-regulatory processes increasingly come into play and self-efficacy is more likely to contribute to the prediction of generalization.

As a preliminary test, we predicted final training performance using selfefficacy and performance on the next to last training trial. It is important to note here that task characteristics were identical across training trials. We found that self-efficacy was not significantly related to final training performance after controlling for prior training performance (DR2 5 .004, DF 5.360, p . .5). This finding is consistent with those of Ackerman et al. (1995) and Mitchell et al. (1994). However, self-efficacy did predict performance after controlling for previous performance when task complexity and difficulty increased. The contribution was reduced in that the zero-order correlation between self-efficacy and adaptive performance was .45, whereas it's b weight after controlling for all prior variables was .20, although this is a very rigorous test. Thus, while there is clearly some redundancy between self-efficacy and prior performance, self-efficacy does account for significant unique variance in adaptive performance beyond that accounted by prior performance.

Our conclusion is that when task characteristics are static, self-efficacy does not add much to the prediction to performance beyond previous skill levels. However, when transfer necessitates the adaptation of knowledge and skills to meet new demands, self-efficacy becomes important. It is under these circumstances that self-efficacy can be expected to influence motivational and selfregulatory processes important for effective transfer. It is relatively rare to find unique contributions to performance for these nontraditional learning indicators, especially self-efficacy, after controlling for performance, learning

ability, and other individual differences (see Ackerman et al., 1995; Martocchio, 1994; Martocchio & Dulebohn, 1994; Martocchio & Webster, 1992; Thomas & Mathieu, 1994). We believe that this relationship warrants further research attention.

A number of studies have demonstrated that knowledge structures have significant relationships with later performance (Acton et al., 1994; Dorsey et al., 1999; Kraiger et al., 1995; Stout et al., 1997). For example, Acton et al. (1994) demonstrated that the knowledge structure of students regarding computer programming concepts was related to exam performance. Similarly, Stout et al. (1997) found that measures of knowledge structures were consistent with the actual performance of teams of naval aviators. However, very few studies have assessed whether measures of knowledge structures and declarative knowledge assess different types of learning. We were able to identify only one study that has attempted such an empirical examination (Stout et al., 1997). They found knowledge structure measures provided information related to training and learning outcomes that was not available from traditional measures. However, we know that both structural and declarative knowledge are likely to be related to previous task performance and self-efficacy. We know of no studies that have attempted to assess the unique impact of declarative and structural knowledge on performance after controlling for previous performance and self-efficacy. Our findings demonstrate that both forms of knowledge are important for generalization of training to new and more complex task environments.

This research has implications for the development of models to guide training design for complex tasks, but considerable work is required before such models can be well-specified. First, the primary focus of our conceptual model is on the development of learning outcomes that enhance adaptability to more complex task situations. Subsequent research efforts should concentrate on elaborating theoretical processes relevant to mastery goal effects that are inferred by this research, but which were not directly addressed. The model posited that mastery goals operate by influencing self-regulatory processes. This research did not directly assess indicators of self-regulation beyond selfefficacy. To provide additional support for the hypothesized theoretical process, we need to expand our assessment to include factors that reference self-monitoring, self-evaluation, and attributions.

Second, we evaluated the independent effects of individual differences in order to yield better assessments of the effects of the training strategies. However, although GPA is often used as an indicator of learning ability, it would be better to use an assessment of general cognitive ability. This is particularly important given the high information processing demands of complex tasks and the well-established relationship between general cognitive ability and complex skill acquisition (Ackerman et al., 1995).

Third, although our goal orientation-based training interventions are consistent with previous manipulations (e.g., Stevens & Gist, 1997; Winters & Latham, 1996), research should continue to investigate the impact and effectiveness of alternative interventions in the initiation and pursuit of learning and performance goals.2 Additionally, we found little impact of trait performance orientation, but this finding is consistent with general patterns in the literature (Beaubien & Payne, 1999). Recent research suggests that performance orientation may be composed of two distinct subdimensions, one that focuses on demonstrating competence while the other focuses on avoidance of failure (Vande-Walle, 1997). Future research should elaborate the effects of these different performance orientations.

Fourth, our indicators of knowledge structure should be further elaborated. We demonstrate that measures of knowledge structure coherence captured a form of learning that is distinct from declarative knowledge and previous levels of skill. However, some might argue that what trainees really need to learn is many very specific productions, leading to compilation and chunking.3 It is not clear that current measure of knowledge structure captures these processes, although some theorists suggest that it may do so (Ford & Kraiger, 1995; Kraiger et al., 1993). Thus, it becomes important to assess more clearly what it is that knowledge structure measures capture and how they relate to compilation and chunking processes. Additional indicators that capture a broader range of procedural skills that are central to effective performance are warranted. The effectiveness of the knowledge structure assessment supports our effort to go beyond basic, information-processing concepts to include concepts that index task strategies and actions. By better integrating these two sources of procedural and strategic knowledge, we believe we can improve the assessment of knowledge compilation for complex tasks.

Fifth, it is possible that we may have reversed the true causal arrows for certain components of our model. However, Cook and Campbell (1979, p. 31) point out that there are three important criteria for inferring causality. The first is covariation between the presumed cause and effect. We have established this with the zero-order correlations as well as with the more conservative and informative regression analyses. The second is temporal precedence. This is easily established for the variables which are measured or manipulated earlier in the study and which could not have been impacted by events that occurred later in the study (e.g., measurement of trait goal orientations prior to task introduction, application of training goal interventions prior to assessment of dependent measures). In fact, the timing of our measurements was entirely consistent with our theoretical model. The third criterion is the need to control for alternative explanations. We employed both experimental and statistical controls to eliminate many possible alternative explanations. For example, we randomly assigned participants to experimental conditions, so it cannot be argued that processes or outcomes influenced the intervention. Additionally,

if we inappropriately reversed the direction of causality on a number of key linkages then this would manifest itself in the omnibus test of our model. Finally, we believe our model is firmly established on previous empirical and theoretical work. For example, because personality is a stable characteristic and it is measured prior to introduction to the task, it is very difficult to make a strong argument that the direction of causality flows in the other direction. However, future studies should add constructs to the emerging nomological network and rigorously test for the possibility of alternative causal patterns.

Finally, our study included primarily college students with a modest sample size. Use of college students may restrict the range of the variance in ability and goal orientation traits, making it difficult to test for aptitude–treatments interactions (ATIs).4 Future studies should attempt to replicate and elaborate our findings using larger and more varied samples performing under a variety of different task conditions. In particular, researchers should explore the possibility of ATIs between ability and mastery/performance interventions (Bell & Kozlowski, 2000).

Mastery training goals evidence promise as an instructional strategy for enhancing knowledge structure coherence, self-efficacy, and performance adaptability to more complex task situations. We caution that additional research to establish generalizability in operational samples and situations is needed. However, with that caveat noted, we see two potential contributions to training design. First, mastery goals provide instructors and team leaders with a flexible training strategy. Leaders and instructors can be easily trained to exhibit the necessary behaviors to provide this type of learning orientation for existing training systems (Kozlowski, Gully, McHugh, Salas, & Cannon-Bowers, 1996). Second, sequenced mastery goals provide a potential means for improving adaptability and resilience in complex task situations. For example, instructional designers can devise a sequence of practice scenarios that progressively orient trainees from basic to more complex knowledge and skill. By better guiding the learning experience, without limiting attention to salient surface characteristics, sequenced mastery goals can enhance learning and self-regulatory capabilities, laying the foundation for adaptive skills (Kozlowski, 1998; Kozlowski, Toney, Mullins, Weissbein, Brown, & Bell, in press; Smith et al., 1997).
